deep.reconstruction:
OVERVIEW. The page is a scratch study of discrete logarithms ('indices') for Gaussian integers. Gauss asks whether complex conjugation can be written as raising to a power k. He tests this on a numerical example, sees that it fails, and replaces it with a two-component exponent mu + nu*k. The facing page then develops this into a 'double base' (M, N).

A. Top left: the naive hypothesis, tested modulo pi = -5+2i.
- 'Man sagt es sei a-bi = (a+bi)^k, kk = 1': conjugation is supposed to be a power map, and since it is an involution, k^2 = 1 for the exponents.
- The modulus pi = -5+2i has norm 25+4 = 29, so Z[i]/pi is F_29.
- [mine] Since 2i = 5 mod pi, we get i = 5*15 = 17 mod 29.
- Then 1+i = 18, which is a primitive root mod 29 (18^14 = -1, 18^4 = 25, not 1).
- 1+4i = 1+68 = 11, and 18^15 = 11. So 1+4i = (1+i)^15 mod pi, as Gauss writes.
- 1-4i = -67 = 20, and 18^20 = 20. So 1-4i = (1+i)^20, again correct.
- The header 'k = 22 mod -5+2i' [mine, verified]: 1-i = -16 = 13 = 18^22. So 22 is the index of 1-i = conj(1+i) to base 1+i, i.e. the k making 1-i = (1+i)^k.
- If conjugation were the power map z -> z^k, then 1-4i = (1+4i)^k = (1+i)^{15k} would require 20 = 15k mod 28.
- With k = 22 this gives 15*22 = 330 = 22 mod 28, which is not 20.
- Also k^2 = 484 = 8 mod 28, not 1.
- So the hypothesis fails. The reason [mine]: conjugation maps the ideal (pi) to (conj pi), so it does not induce a map of Z[i]/pi to itself.
- Gauss's struck line and '20 ... 15k' record this check. Under it, '-5+2k' rewrites the modulus with k in place of i.

B. Right column: the corrected definition (two-component exponents).
- Define (x+iy)^(mu+nu k) = X+iY to mean two conditions:
  (1) (xx+yy)^mu = XX+YY;
  (2) ((x+iy)/(x-iy))^nu = (X+iY)/(X-iY).
- In words, mu acts on the norm and nu acts on the 'argument' z/zbar.
- The middle formula gives an explicit realization: z^(mu+nu k) = z^((mu+nu)/2) * zbar^((mu-nu)/2).
- [check] The norm of this is N^((mu+nu)/2 + (mu-nu)/2) = N^mu. The quotient by its conjugate is (z/zbar)^nu. Both conditions hold.
- 'Also': z^k (mu = 0, nu = 1) is the X+iY with norm 1 and the same z/zbar. So the unit 1 governs the norm part and k governs the unimodular part; the ordinary z itself is z^(1+k).
- Exponents are taken modulo different periods: mu is determined mod p-1, nu mod p+1.
- This fits a rational prime p = 3 mod 4. There (Z[i]/p)* has order p^2-1, the norms form F_p* (order p-1), and the norm-1 subgroup has order p+1.
- Gauss notes 'p mu = mu, p nu = -nu'. [mine] For inert p, Frobenius z^p = zbar fixes the norm and inverts z/zbar. So multiplying the exponent by p acts as mu+nu k -> mu-nu k, i.e. as conjugation.
- The last lines, 'oder wenn ... 2' and 'mu'+nu'k = mu+nu k mod (a-bk)', try to express the double periodicity as a single congruence in the ring Z[k]/(k^2-1). The factor 2 probably refers to the parity condition forced by the 1/2's.
- [mine] With zbar = z^p, one has z^(mu+nu k) = z^(((1+p)mu + (1-p)nu)/2). This agrees with the norm condition mod p-1 only when mu - nu is even.
- Writing 'aa+bb = p' in the same column is inconsistent with the period p+1. It belongs to the split case of part A/C.

C. Bottom left: double base for the split prime p = 41 = 5^2 + 4^2, pi = 5+4i.
- g is the original primitive root ('Anfaengl.', initial).
- New bases h, H are chosen with h^5 H^4 = 1 mod 5+4i, i.e. 5 log h + 4 log H = 0 (mod 40, the order of the group).
- He takes h = g^4 and H = g^(-5). Then h^5 H^4 = g^(20-20) = 1, which is correct.
- These are exactly the inverses of the next page's M = g^(p-1-b) = g^36 = g^-4 and N = g^a = g^5, which satisfy M^a N^b = 1.
- '5t+4u mod 41' is the corresponding linear form on pairs of exponents. [mine] Modulo 5+4i one has i = 9 (since 9^2 = 81 = -1 and 5+36 = 41).
- This leads to the next page's idea: if L = M^mu N^nu mod pi, then set 'lg L = mu + nu i mod pi'.

OVERALL. Gauss is searching for a 'logarithm' with values in a quadratic ring, using a two-element basis instead of a single primitive root. The facing page sums this up: 'Die ZWEIHEIT muss immer die Hauptsache bleiben' (the twoness must always remain the main thing).
errors: The opening hypothesis a-bi = (a+bi)^k mod a Gaussian prime pi is false in general, because conjugation does not preserve the ideal (pi). Gauss's own check refutes it: k = 22 is forced by 1-i = (1+i)^22, but then 15k = 22, not 20, mod 28, and k^2 = 8, not 1, mod 28. This is a tested-and-rejected hypothesis, not a slip.

'log H = 5' together with 'H = 1/g^5' is a sign slip: log H = -5 (= 35 mod 40). Also, the condition 5 log h + 4 log H must vanish mod 40 (= p-1), not 'durch 41'. With log H = +5 one gets 40, divisible by 40 but not by 41; with -5 one gets 0.

'aa+bb = p' sits beside the rule 'nu mod p+1' and 'p nu = -nu', which only make sense for an inert prime p = 3 mod 4. In the split case p = a^2+b^2 the norm-1 part has order p-1. The column mixes the two cases.

The realization z^((mu+nu)/2) zbar^((mu-nu)/2) needs mu = nu mod 2 (or division by 2 in the exponent group). This is presumably the point of the marginal '2'. The final congruence mod (a-bk) is not justified on the page.

results.what: Numerical indices modulo the Gaussian prime -5+2i (norm 29) with primitive root 1+i: 1+4i = (1+i)^15, 1-4i = (1+i)^20, 1-i = (1+i)^22.
results.modern_name: discrete logarithm / index table in Z[i]/(pi), identified with F_29
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (primitive roots for complex moduli, Theoria residuorum biquadraticorum, 1832); Jacobi's Canon arithmeticus for rational indices

results.what: Recognition that complex conjugation is not a power map modulo a split Gaussian prime.
results.modern_name: conjugation interchanges pi and pibar; it is not an automorphism of Z[i]/(pi)

results.what: For an inert prime p, a unit z of Z[i]/p is described by an exponent pair (mu mod p-1, nu mod p+1) via norm and z/zbar. Frobenius acts as nu -> -nu (z^p = zbar).
results.modern_name: decomposition of (F_{p^2})* into norm part F_p* and norm-one torus (order p+1); Frobenius acting by inversion on the norm-one torus
results.usually_credited_to: Galois/Dedekind-era finite-field theory; the norm-one torus is modern language

results.what: Two-component 'logarithm' mu + nu k with k^2 = 1, i.e. exponents in Z[k]/(k^2-1); z^(mu+nu k) = z^((mu+nu)/2) zbar^((mu-nu)/2).
results.modern_name: exponents in a split quadratic algebra (idempotents (1+-k)/2); module structure of the unit group over a group ring Z[Gal]
results.usually_credited_to: much later (Galois-module viewpoint, Stickelberger/Hilbert era and after)

results.what: Double base for a split prime p = a^2+b^2: h = g^4, H = g^(-5) with h^5 H^4 = 1 mod 5+4i (p = 41); on the next page, logarithms valued mod pi as mu + nu i.
results.modern_name: choosing a basis adapted to the relation a*x + b*y = 0; logarithm with values in Z[i]/pi

deep.surprise_reason: Gauss's work with indices and primitive roots for Gaussian moduli is well documented. The new element is an exploratory, partly inconsistent attempt at a two-component 'logarithm' that separates norm and argument (the norm-one torus) and treats Frobenius as exponent conjugation. It is interesting as a glimpse of his 'Zweiheit' programme, but it is a fragmentary sketch with no finished theorem.

checkable.asserts: with g = 6 primitive mod 41, h = g^4 and H = g^-5 satisfy h^5 H^4 = 1

checkable.sympy: len([1 for x in range(7) for y in range(7) if (x*x + y*y) % 7 == 1]) == 8
checkable.asserts: for inert p = 7 the norm-one subgroup of (Z[i]/p)* has order p+1
the norm of z^((mu+nu)/2) zbar^((mu-nu)/2) is N(z)^mu (with w = zbar; z, w positive symbols)

transcription_corrections: The header 'k = 22 mod -5+2i' is the index of 1-i to base 1+i modulo -5+2i, not an independent definition.
The line '20 [?] 15k' is the test congruence 20 = 15k (mod 28), which fails. '-5+2k' beneath it is the modulus -5+2i rewritten with k.
'durch [-21-] 41': the corrected number appears to be 41, but mathematically 40 (= p-1) is what is required.
'g Anfaengl. Modulus' presumably means the original primitive root g (cf. next page 'ursprüngliche Radix primitiva'); the word read as 'Modulus' is uncertain.
'oder wenn [?] 2' is followed by 'mu'+nu'k = mu+nu k mod (a-bk)'. The reading (a-bk) is plausible, but the line is unclear.
